events.description: 7. Judge Brian E. Murphy: ELECTRONIC ORDER entered. To the extent Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, see generally Dkt. 2, also intended to seek a Temporary Restraining order, see Dkt. 1 at 5 (complaint seeking both a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction); see also Rodi v. S. New Eng. Sch. of L., 389 F.3d 5, 13 (1st Cir. 2004) (explaining that courts should generally construe pro se pleadings liberally), the motion fails to demonstrate that “immediate and irreparable” harm will occur “before the adverse party can be heard in opposition,” as required for a temporary restraining order issued without notice, Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(b)(1)(A). As such, the Court will not issue a temporary restraining order.The Court ORDERS Plaintiff to serve on Defendants a copy of Plaintiff’s Complaint, Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, all supporting documents filed in this case, and a copy of this Order no later than Friday, July 24, 2026. Defendants shall file a response to the Motion for Preliminary Injunction no later than August 7, 2026. (MBM) (Entered: 07/21/2026)

events.description: 35. Judge Brian E. Murphy: ORDER entered. ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE by November 19, 2026, for why this Court should not dismiss the case for the reasons stated in Defendants’ motion and for why the Court should consider an opposition filed after the deadline. Defendants Blanche and Dhillon moved to dismiss the case pursuant to Rule 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure on October 29, 2026. Dkt. 33. Accordingly, Plaintiff’s opposition was due on November 12, 2026. See L.R. 7.1(b)(2) (providing 14 days to file an opposition). Plaintiff filed neither a response nor a motion to continue. However, given the First Circuit's caution that dismissal as a sanction “is strong medicine, not casually to be dispensed,” Tower Ventures, Inc. v. City of Westfield, 296 F.3d 43, 46 (1st Cir. 2002), and “the strong presumption in favor of deciding cases on the merits,” United States ex rel. Nargol v. DePuy Orthopaedics, Inc., 69 F.4th 1, 12 (1st Cir. 2023) (quoting Malot v. Dorado Beach Cottages Assocs., 478 F.3d 40, 43 (1st Cir. 2007)), the Court will afford Plaintiff until close of business on Thursday, November 19, 2026, to file a response to this Order to Show Cause. Absent a response, the case will be dismissed for failure to prosecute. See Tower Ventures, 296 F.3d at 45 (“[D]isobedience of court orders, in and of itself, constitutes extreme misconduct (and, thus, warrants dismissal).”). Though Plaintiff appears pro se and is therefore entitled to some latitude, see Dutil v. Murphy, 550 F.3d 154, 158 (1st Cir. 2008), “pro se status does not free a litigant in a civil case of the obligation to comply with procedural rules,” Goguen v. Allen, 780 F.3d 437, 457 n.58 (1st Cir. 2015) (quoting Ruiz Rivera v. Riley, 209 F.3d 24, 28 (1st Cir. 2000), abrogated on other grounds by Casanova v. Dubois, 289 F.3d 142 (1st Cir. 2002)). (MBM) (Entered: 11/16/2026)

events.description: 36. Judge Brian E. Murphy: ELECTRONIC ORDER entered. On November 16, 2026, the Court issued an order requiring Plaintiff to show cause by November 19, 2026, “for why this Court should not dismiss the case for the reasons stated in Defendants’ motion and for why the Court should consider an opposition filed after the deadline.” Dkt. 35 . That deadline has passed without a response from Plaintiff. The Court’s order noted that “[a]bsent a response, the case will be dismissed for failure to prosecute.” Id. Accordingly, this case is dismissed for failure to prosecute. (MBM) (Entered: 11/20/2026)
